what_its_for: Budesonide is a steroid medicine that reduces swelling and irritation in your body. Depending on the form you are prescribed, it can treat asthma, nasal allergies (like hay fever), Crohn's disease, or ulcerative colitis. It works by calming down inflammation so your symptoms get better.
how_to_take: How you take budesonide depends on the form your doctor prescribed: (1) Inhaler (Pulmicort): Breathe it in through your mouth using the inhaler device. Rinse your mouth with water and spit it out after each use to prevent a mouth infection called thrush. (2) Nasal spray (Rhinocort): Spray it into your nostrils. Blow your nose gently before using it. Shake the bottle well and prime it before first use. Avoid spraying into your eyes. (3) Capsules or tablets (Entocort EC, Uceris): Swallow whole with a full glass of water. Do NOT crush, chew, or break the capsules or tablets. Take on an empty stomach if possible or as directed by your doctor. Always follow your doctor or pharmacist's specific instructions for your form of budesonide.
dosing: Your dose will be set by your doctor based on your condition, age, and how you respond to treatment. Do NOT change your dose without talking to your doctor first. For asthma inhalers, typical adult doses range from 180 to 720 micrograms per day. For nasal spray, the usual adult dose is 1 to 4 sprays in each nostril once daily. For capsules or tablets, doses for gut conditions are usually 6 to 9 mg per day. Always use the lowest dose that controls your symptoms, as directed by your doctor.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do NOT double up or take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are not sure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store budesonide at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do NOT store it in the bathroom. Keep the inhaler cap closed when not in use. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine after the expiration date printed on the package. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of unused medicine.
what_to_avoid: Avoid being around people who are sick with infections like chickenpox, measles, or the flu, especially if you are taking higher doses, as budesonide can weaken your immune system. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice if you are taking the capsule or tablet form, as it can increase the amount of medicine in your blood. Do not stop taking budesonide suddenly without talking to your doctor first, especially if you have been on it for a long time. Avoid drinking alcohol while taking budesonide capsules or tablets, as it may increase side effects.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you notice: white patches or sores in your mouth or throat (possible thrush from inhaler use), vision problems or eye pain, signs of infection such as fever, chills, or unusual tiredness, swelling of your face, lips, or throat, worsening breathing or wheezing after using your inhaler, stomach pain, nausea, or blood in your stool, signs of low cortisol levels such as extreme tiredness, weakness, dizziness, or fainting, or if your symptoms do not improve after a few weeks of treatment. Seek emergency help immediately if you have a severe allergic reaction including hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face or throat.
when_it_works: Budesonide does not work right away. For the nasal spray, you may start to notice improvement in nasal symptoms within 1 to 3 days, but full benefits may take up to 2 weeks. For the inhaler used for asthma, it may take 1 to 2 weeks of regular use before you feel the full benefit. For capsules or tablets treating gut conditions, you may start to feel better within 2 to 4 weeks. It is very important to keep using it every day as prescribed, even if you feel fine, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Children: Budesonide inhalers and nasal sprays can be used in children, but doses are lower. Long-term use in children should be monitored by a doctor as it may slow growth slightly. Older adults: Use with caution as older patients may be more sensitive to side effects like bone thinning (osteoporosis). Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Talk to your doctor before using budesonide. Inhaled and nasal forms are generally considered safer during pregnancy than oral forms, but always check with your healthcare provider first. Patients with liver disease: The capsule and tablet forms may be stronger in people with liver problems. Tell your doctor if you have liver disease so your dose can be adjusted. Patients with infections: Tell your doctor if you have any current infections, including tuberculosis or fungal infections, as budesonide can make infections harder to fight.
